title: Congenital and Genetic Neurological Diseases
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers inherited and prenatal disorders that injure the nervous system: chromosomal and repeat disorders (Down syndrome, fragile X), leukodystrophies, lysosomal storage diseases, amino acid and urea cycle defects, acute intermittent porphyria, Wilson disease, and the congenital infections and toxins that cause microcephaly. Board questions give an infant or child with a pattern of findings and ask for the missing enzyme or gene, the substance that accumulates, the mode of inheritance, or the single clue that separates two look-alike diseases. If you can trace each disease from the defect to what builds up, which cells store it, and why those cells fail, the clinical picture follows logically.
prerequisites: Meiosis, nondisjunction, and patterns of Mendelian and X-linked inheritance (NE-16)
Lysosomal and peroxisomal function and sphingolipid structure
Amino acid catabolism, the urea cycle, and heme synthesis
Myelin formation by oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells

connections.how: Nondisjunction, Robertsonian translocation, trinucleotide repeat expansion, and X inactivation explain how these diseases arise and who expresses them.
Each inborn error is a blocked step in a pathway, so the substrate before the block accumulates and the product after it becomes deficient.

connections.to: Hepatic encephalopathy and metabolic brain injury (NE-14, NE-20-D)
connections.how: Ammonia neurotoxicity in urea cycle defects uses the same astrocyte glutamine mechanism as liver failure.
Amyloid in Down syndrome, basal ganglia injury in Wilson disease, and GBA variants in Parkinson disease link genetics to adult degeneration.
Congenital CMV, rubella, toxoplasmosis, Zika, and ethanol injure neural progenitors during brain growth, producing microcephaly.

terms.def: Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during meiosis or mitosis, producing gametes or cells with an extra or missing chromosome.
A disorder in which loss of a lysosomal hydrolase traps its undegraded substrate inside lysosomes, enlarging and damaging the cells that turn that substrate over.
An inherited disorder of white matter in which myelin is abnormally formed or progressively destroyed.
A membrane-bound organelle that, among other tasks, shortens very long chain fatty acids by beta oxidation before mitochondria finish them.
A membrane lipid built on a ceramide backbone; gangliosides, cerebrosides, sulfatides, and sphingomyelin are examples.
A red fovea framed by pale, swollen retina, seen when lipid-filled ganglion cells surround the fovea, which has no ganglion cells.
An increase in the number of copies of a three-base sequence beyond a stable range, often growing further in successive generations (anticipation).
An elevated blood ammonia concentration, toxic to the brain, from failure of urea synthesis or liver clearance.
A liver-made ferroxidase that carries most circulating copper; copper must be loaded onto it by ATP7B, or the apoprotein is rapidly degraded.
A head circumference more than 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and sex, usually reflecting a small brain.

sections.title: Down syndrome: neurologic and associated features

blocks.text: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability. About 95% of cases arise from meiotic nondisjunction, most often in maternal meiosis I, which is why risk rises with maternal age. About 4% result from a Robertsonian translocation, usually between chromosomes 14 and 21, which can be inherited from a balanced carrier parent and is independent of maternal age; the rest are mosaic, with milder and more variable features.

The extra copy of chromosome 21 raises the dosage of every gene on it by about 50%. Brain growth and neuronal development are altered, producing intellectual disability that is usually mild to moderate, and hypotonia that is often the first sign in the newborn. Gene dosage also explains early-onset Alzheimer disease. The amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene lies on chromosome 21, so lifelong overproduction of APP yields more amyloid beta. Plaques and tangles are present in nearly all adults with Down syndrome by about age 40, and clinical dementia commonly appears in the 50s.

Several features reflect abnormal connective tissue and embryonic development. Laxity of the transverse ligament of the atlas allows atlantoaxial instability, so C1 can slip on C2 and compress the cervical cord, causing neck pain, gait change, hyperreflexia, or weakness. Failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse produces the atrioventricular septal defect, the most characteristic heart lesion. Failed recanalization of the duodenum gives duodenal atresia, with bilious vomiting and a double bubble on radiograph. Leukemia risk is increased: acute lymphoblastic leukemia is more frequent overall, while acute megakaryoblastic leukemia is especially increased in children under 5 and may be preceded in newborns by a transient myeloproliferative disorder linked to GATA1 mutations.

blocks.text: Prenatal screening reflects the same biology. In the second trimester quadruple screen, alpha-fetoprotein and estriol are low while hCG and inhibin A are high; in the first trimester, nuchal translucency is increased, hCG is high, and PAPP-A is low. Karyotype distinguishes free trisomy from translocation, which matters because a translocation carrier parent has a high recurrence risk.

blocks.predict: A 45-year-old with Down syndrome develops progressive memory loss. Why would her Alzheimer pathology appear decades earlier than in the general population?
blocks.explain: The APP gene is on chromosome 21. Three copies raise APP and amyloid beta production from birth, so plaques form early and nearly all adults have Alzheimer neuropathology by about 40.

sections.title: Leukodystrophies: adrenoleukodystrophy, metachromatic leukodystrophy, and Krabbe disease

blocks.text: Myelin is a lipid-rich membrane made by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves, and it is turned over continuously. A leukodystrophy results when a defect in lipid handling makes myelin unstable or poisons the cells that make it. The three classic disorders differ in the organelle involved (peroxisome or lysosome), the stored lipid, the inheritance, and whether peripheral nerve and adrenal gland are also affected.
X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy

ABCD1 encodes a transporter in the peroxisomal membrane that imports very long chain fatty acids (VLCFA, 22 or more carbons) for beta oxidation. Mitochondria cannot shorten these fatty acids, so when ABCD1 fails they accumulate in plasma, myelin, and the adrenal cortex and Leydig cells. In the childhood cerebral form, a previously normal boy aged about 4 to 10 develops behavior change, school decline, visual and hearing loss, and spasticity, with inflammatory demyelination that usually begins in the posterior (parieto-occipital) white matter. Adrenal insufficiency with hyperpigmentation may precede neurologic signs, so primary adrenal insufficiency in a boy should prompt VLCFA measurement. Adult men may instead develop adrenomyeloneuropathy, a slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, and many carrier women develop a milder myelopathy.
Metachromatic leukodystrophy and Krabbe disease

Both are autosomal recessive lysosomal diseases of galactolipids that destroy central and peripheral myelin, so upper motor neuron signs coexist with peripheral neuropathy (reduced reflexes, slowed nerve conduction). In metachromatic leukodystrophy, arylsulfatase A deficiency leaves sulfatides (cerebroside sulfate) undegraded; the stored material stains metachromatically, a color shift with certain dyes that gives the disease its name, and urinary sulfatides are increased. The late infantile form presents in the second year with gait disturbance and regression. In Krabbe disease, galactocerebrosidase deficiency allows psychosine (galactosylsphingosine) to accumulate, which is directly toxic to oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells. Myelin collapses early, so infants at about 3 to 6 months show irritability, stiffness, optic atrophy, and neuropathy. Galactocerebroside is phagocytosed by macrophages that fuse into multinucleated globoid cells, the histologic hallmark.

blocks.title: Comparing the three leukodystrophies
blocks.caption: Peroxisomal disease adds adrenal failure; lysosomal galactolipid diseases add peripheral neuropathy.

sections.title: Phenylketonuria: phenylalanine hydroxylase and BH4 deficiency

blocks.text: Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), a liver enzyme, converts phenylalanine to tyrosine using tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as cofactor. In classic phenylketonuria (PKU), an autosomal recessive PAH deficiency, phenylalanine accumulates and tyrosine can no longer be made, so tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid. Excess phenylalanine is transaminated to phenylpyruvate and further to phenyllactate and phenylacetate, the phenylketones that appear in urine; phenylacetate gives sweat and urine a musty or mousy odor.

blocks.title: From PAH block to brain injury
steps: PAH or BH4 deficient; phenylalanine cannot become tyrosine
Plasma phenylalanine rises; tyrosine falls
Phenylalanine saturates the LAT1 transporter at the blood-brain barrier
Brain uptake of tyrosine, tryptophan, and other large neutral amino acids falls
Brain protein, myelin, dopamine, and serotonin synthesis impaired
Intellectual disability, seizures, behavior problems
blocks.caption: High phenylalanine competes with other large neutral amino acids for the same transporter during brain development.

blocks.text: The brain injury comes mainly from high phenylalanine itself. It competes for the large neutral amino acid transporter (LAT1) at the blood-brain barrier, starving developing neurons of tyrosine and tryptophan needed for protein, dopamine, and serotonin synthesis, and it impairs myelination. Untreated infants appear normal at birth because maternal metabolism cleared phenylalanine in utero; over months they develop intellectual disability, seizures, hyperactivity, and eczema. Fair skin, hair, and blue eyes reflect reduced melanin, because less tyrosine is available and phenylalanine competitively inhibits tyrosinase. Newborn screening measures blood phenylalanine after protein feeding has begun.

About 1 to 2% of cases are caused by defects in BH4 synthesis or recycling (for example dihydropteridine reductase deficiency). BH4 is also the cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase, so these infants lack dopamine and serotonin even when phenylalanine is controlled, and neurologic deterioration is more severe. The classic exam point is that a BH4 defect causes neurologic decline out of proportion to the phenylalanine level, because neurotransmitter synthesis fails directly.

Maternal PKU affects a genetically normal fetus. If a woman with PKU has high phenylalanine during pregnancy, it crosses the placenta, which actively concentrates amino acids, and acts as a teratogen. The infant shows microcephaly, intellectual disability, growth restriction, and congenital heart defects, even though the infant does not have PKU.

blocks.title: Classic PKU versus BH4 deficiency
blocks.caption: BH4 is shared by three aromatic amino acid hydroxylases, so its loss affects neurotransmitter synthesis directly.

blocks.text: Lysosomal hydrolases remove one group at a time from complex lipids. When one is missing, its substrate is trapped in lysosomes of whichever cells normally degrade it, so the distribution of the substrate predicts which organs fail. Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick disease both cause infantile neurodegeneration and a cherry-red macula, and both are autosomal recessive with a higher carrier frequency in Ashkenazi Jewish populations, so the distinction rests on the enzyme, the substrate, and the presence of hepatosplenomegaly.

In Tay-Sachs disease, mutations in HEXA eliminate hexosaminidase A, and GM2 ganglioside accumulates. Gangliosides are concentrated in neuronal membranes, so neurons swell with lysosomes containing concentric lamellar (onion-skin) membranous bodies. Infants are normal until about 3 to 6 months, then show weakness, loss of milestones, an exaggerated startle to sound, blindness, and seizures, with death in early childhood. Because visceral macrophages handle little GM2, the liver and spleen are not enlarged.

In Niemann-Pick disease types A and B, deficiency of acid sphingomyelinase (gene SMPD1) leaves sphingomyelin undegraded. Sphingomyelin is abundant in cell membranes that macrophages engulf, so lipid-laden foam cells fill the liver, spleen, marrow, and lungs, producing massive hepatosplenomegaly. Type A is the infantile neuronopathic form, with feeding difficulty, regression, and death by about age 3; type B spares the brain and presents with hepatosplenomegaly and lung disease. Niemann-Pick type C is a different disease, a defect in cholesterol trafficking (NPC1 or NPC2) that typically presents later with ataxia, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, and dementia.

The cherry-red spot arises the same way in both. Retinal ganglion cells swollen with stored lipid make the perimacular retina pale and opaque, while the fovea, which contains no ganglion cells, lets the red choroid show through.

blocks.title: Tay-Sachs versus Niemann-Pick type A
rows: Foam cells; zebra bodies on electron microscopy
blocks.caption: Hepatosplenomegaly is the single most useful discriminator.

blocks.predict: Why does Niemann-Pick disease enlarge the spleen while Tay-Sachs does not, when both enzymes are missing from every cell?
blocks.explain: Organ involvement follows substrate turnover, not enzyme distribution. Macrophages degrade large amounts of sphingomyelin from engulfed membranes, so they fill with it. GM2 ganglioside is concentrated in neurons, so only neurons store it.

sections.title: Fabry, Gaucher, Hurler, and Hunter diseases

blocks.text: These lysosomal diseases follow the same rule as the previous section: the substrate collects in the cells that degrade it, and symptoms follow from those cells. Two of them are X-linked (Fabry and Hunter); the others, like most lysosomal diseases, are autosomal recessive.
Fabry disease

Deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A (gene GLA) causes globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) to accumulate in vascular endothelium and smooth muscle, dorsal root ganglion neurons, podocytes, and cardiac myocytes. Storage in small sensory fibers and their ganglia produces the earliest symptom, a small fiber neuropathy with burning pain in the hands and feet (acroparesthesias) that begins in childhood and is provoked by heat, fever, or exercise. Autonomic involvement reduces sweating, so heat intolerance is common. Skin vessels form angiokeratomas, small dark red papules clustered between the umbilicus and knees. Vasculopathy causes early stroke, often in the posterior circulation, along with proteinuria progressing to kidney failure and left ventricular hypertrophy. Corneal whorls (verticillata) are a useful eye clue. Because of random X inactivation, heterozygous women are often symptomatic, usually later and more mildly than men.
Gaucher disease

Glucocerebrosidase deficiency (gene GBA) leaves glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide) in macrophages, which become Gaucher cells with a crumpled tissue paper cytoplasm. Type 1, the most common form and frequent among Ashkenazi Jewish people, spares the brain: hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia from marrow replacement and hypersplenism, bone pain, avascular necrosis of the femoral head, and Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the distal femur. Types 2 and 3 are neuronopathic. Type 2 is acute infantile disease with rapid brainstem dysfunction and death in early childhood; type 3 progresses more slowly, with impaired horizontal saccades (supranuclear gaze palsy), seizures, and ataxia. Heterozygous GBA variants also raise the risk of Parkinson disease.
Hurler and Hunter syndromes

These mucopolysaccharidoses store dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate, glycosaminoglycans of connective tissue and cell surfaces, so they distort bone, face, airway, heart valves, viscera, and brain, and glycosaminoglycans appear in urine. Hurler syndrome (MPS I) is autosomal recessive alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency with coarse facies, corneal clouding, progressive developmental decline, hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal dysostosis multiplex, and airway obstruction. Hunter syndrome (MPS II) is X-linked recessive iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, generally milder and more variable, with aggressive behavior in some boys and no corneal clouding.

sections.title: Wilson disease: copper transport and basal ganglia injury

blocks.text: Dietary copper is absorbed in the intestine and carried to the liver, which excretes it almost entirely into bile. In the hepatocyte, the copper-transporting ATPase ATP7B, encoded on chromosome 13, does two jobs: it loads copper onto apoceruloplasmin in the trans-Golgi network, and it moves excess copper into bile. Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is autosomal recessive loss of ATP7B. Copper cannot be excreted, so it accumulates first in the liver, and apoceruloplasmin that receives no copper is rapidly degraded, so serum ceruloplasmin is low.

blocks.title: Copper overload in Wilson disease
steps: ATP7B mutation in hepatocytes
Copper not excreted into bile or loaded onto ceruloplasmin
Hepatocyte copper rises; free radical injury; hepatitis, cirrhosis
Free (non-ceruloplasmin) copper spills into blood
Copper deposits in basal ganglia, cornea, and kidney
Movement disorder, psychiatric change, Kayser-Fleischer rings
blocks.caption: The liver fails first; extrahepatic deposition follows when hepatic storage is overwhelmed.

blocks.text: Free copper catalyzes formation of hydroxyl radicals (Fenton chemistry), injuring mitochondria and membranes. Hepatic disease, from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or acute liver failure, usually appears in childhood or adolescence. Sudden release of copper from necrotic hepatocytes can cause Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, and renal tubular deposits can produce a Fanconi-type defect.

Neurologic disease usually presents in the late teens to 30s. Copper damages the lenticular nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus), along with thalamus and brainstem, disrupting basal ganglia motor circuits. The result is tremor (classically a coarse, proximal wing-beating tremor), dystonia, rigidity and bradykinesia, dysarthria, drooling, and incoordination. Injury to frontal-striatal circuits explains psychiatric change, including depression, personality change, impulsivity, and psychosis, which may precede the motor signs. Kayser-Fleischer rings are golden-brown copper deposits in Descemet membrane at the corneal margin; they are present in nearly all patients with neurologic disease but in only about half of those with hepatic disease alone.

blocks.title: Why serum copper is low in a copper overload disease
blocks.text: A 19-year-old with tremor and dysarthria has low serum ceruloplasmin, low total serum copper, and high 24-hour urine copper. Step 1: about 90% of serum copper is normally bound to ceruloplasmin. Step 2: without ATP7B, apoceruloplasmin is not loaded and is degraded, so ceruloplasmin and the bound copper fall, lowering total serum copper. Step 3: the unbound (free) copper fraction is actually increased, because the overloaded liver releases it. Step 4: free copper is filtered by the kidney, so urine copper rises, and it deposits in tissues. Total serum copper therefore misleads; ceruloplasmin, urine copper, and liver copper reflect the true overload.

blocks.title: Laboratory and imaging findings in Wilson disease
blocks.caption: Ceruloplasmin is low because it is unloaded, not because copper is scarce.

sections.title: Fragile X syndrome: repeat expansion and gene silencing

blocks.text: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, and the most common single-gene cause of autism. Down syndrome is more common overall, but it is usually a new nondisjunction event rather than an inherited change. Fragile X results from expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the 5 prime untranslated region of FMR1 on the X chromosome.

Normal alleles carry fewer than about 45 repeats. Premutation alleles (about 55 to 200 repeats) are unstable and tend to expand when passed through a mother's meiosis, which explains anticipation: severity increases over generations, but only through female transmission. A full mutation, above about 200 repeats, triggers methylation of the repeat and the CpG island of the FMR1 promoter. The methylated promoter is silenced, so no FMR1 protein (FMRP) is made. The disease is therefore caused by loss of function through epigenetic silencing, not by a toxic protein.

blocks.title: From CGG expansion to synaptic dysfunction
steps: Premutation expands during maternal meiosis
More than about 200 CGG repeats in FMR1
Promoter CpG island hypermethylated
FMR1 transcription silenced; FMRP absent
Unregulated synaptic protein synthesis; immature dendritic spines
Intellectual disability, autism features, seizures
blocks.caption: Fragile X is a loss of function disorder caused by epigenetic silencing.

blocks.text: FMRP is an RNA-binding protein that normally restrains local translation of specific messenger RNAs at synapses, in part downstream of group I metabotropic glutamate receptors. Without it, protein synthesis at synapses is excessive and unregulated, dendritic spines remain long, thin, and immature, and synaptic plasticity is abnormal. Boys with the full mutation show moderate intellectual disability, autism features (gaze avoidance, hand flapping, social anxiety), hyperactivity, and seizures in some. Physical features include a long narrow face, prominent jaw, large protruding ears, joint laxity, and macroorchidism that becomes evident after puberty; mitral valve prolapse also occurs. Females with a full mutation are affected more mildly and variably because of X inactivation.

Premutation carriers do not have fragile X syndrome but have distinct risks: primary ovarian insufficiency in women and fragile X-associated tremor and ataxia syndrome in older men, both attributed to toxic effects of the overproduced repeat-containing RNA. Diagnosis uses PCR and Southern blot to size the repeat and assess methylation; the cytogenetic fragile site that named the disease is no longer used for diagnosis.

sections.title: Maple syrup urine disease and ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency

blocks.text: Both disorders present as a neonatal encephalopathy: an infant who is well at birth becomes lethargic, feeds poorly, vomits, and may seize or become comatose within days, once protein feeding delivers a substrate load the blocked pathway cannot handle. The toxic molecule differs.
Maple syrup urine disease

The branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine are first transaminated to their alpha-ketoacids, which are then oxidatively decarboxylated by the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. This mitochondrial complex resembles pyruvate dehydrogenase and uses the same cofactors (thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoate, coenzyme A, FAD, and NAD+). In maple syrup urine disease, an autosomal recessive deficiency of this complex, the amino acids and their ketoacids accumulate. Leucine and its ketoacid are the most neurotoxic: leucine competes with other large neutral amino acids for brain uptake, and accumulation causes cerebral edema. Infants show poor feeding, alternating hypotonia and hypertonia, opisthotonus, seizures, and ketoacidosis. The sweet, maple syrup odor of urine and cerumen comes from a compound derived from isoleucine; plasma alloisoleucine is diagnostic.
Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency

Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine in the mitochondria to form citrulline. OTC deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder and the only urea cycle disorder inherited in an X-linked pattern, so affected boys present as newborns while heterozygous girls may have episodes later, after protein loads or illness. Ammonia rises because nitrogen cannot be converted to urea, and unused carbamoyl phosphate leaves the mitochondrion and enters cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis, producing excess orotic acid in urine.

blocks.title: How hyperammonemia injures the brain
steps: Urea cycle blocked; blood ammonia rises
Ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier
Astrocyte glutamine synthetase converts ammonia and glutamate to glutamine
Glutamine accumulates; astrocytes swell osmotically
Cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure
Vomiting, lethargy, seizures, coma
blocks.caption: Ammonia also stimulates the respiratory center, so early hyperammonemia often causes respiratory alkalosis.

blocks.title: Separating OTC deficiency from look-alikes
blocks.text: A 3-day-old boy has vomiting, lethargy, high ammonia, normal anion gap, and high urine orotic acid. Step 1: high ammonia without ketoacidosis points to a urea cycle defect rather than an organic acidemia or maple syrup urine disease. Step 2: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency also causes hyperammonemia, but carbamoyl phosphate is not made, so orotic acid is not increased. Step 3: hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency) raises orotic acid but causes megaloblastic anemia, not hyperammonemia. Step 4: hyperammonemia plus orotic aciduria in a boy fits OTC deficiency.

Heme synthesis begins in the mitochondria, where aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthase joins glycine and succinyl CoA to form ALA; this is the rate-limiting step. In the liver, the ALAS1 isoform is normally held in check by heme through negative feedback. ALA dehydratase then forms porphobilinogen (PBG), and porphobilinogen deaminase (also called hydroxymethylbilane synthase) joins four PBG molecules into the linear tetrapyrrole hydroxymethylbilane, which later steps convert to porphyrins and heme.

Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is autosomal dominant partial deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase, about 50% of normal activity. Most carriers never have symptoms, because the remaining enzyme meets ordinary demand. Attacks occur when hepatic heme demand rises and ALAS1 is induced. Cytochrome P450 enzymes are heme proteins, so drugs that induce them (barbiturates, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, griseofulvin) consume heme and release ALAS1 from feedback. Alcohol and smoking act similarly. Fasting and low carbohydrate intake induce ALAS1 through the same signals that drive gluconeogenesis, which is also why glucose suppresses it. Progesterone induces ALAS1, so attacks are more common in women after puberty and in the luteal phase. With the deaminase step limiting, ALA and PBG pile up behind the block.

blocks.title: Trigger to attack in acute intermittent porphyria
steps: Trigger: P450 inducer, alcohol, fasting, or progesterone
Hepatic heme falls or demand rises; ALAS1 induced
ALA production increases sharply
Partial PBG deaminase deficiency becomes rate limiting
ALA and PBG accumulate in blood and urine
Neurovisceral attack: pain, neuropathy, psychiatric change
blocks.caption: The block is partial, so symptoms appear only when ALA synthesis is driven above what the remaining enzyme can process.

blocks.text: The manifestations are neurologic. ALA is neurotoxic and resembles GABA, and heme deficiency in neurons may also contribute. Autonomic neuropathy produces the dominant symptom, severe poorly localized abdominal pain with nausea, vomiting, and constipation, often with tachycardia and hypertension; the abdomen is soft because the pain is neuropathic, not inflammatory. A motor axonal neuropathy can follow, often proximal and in the arms first, and can progress to respiratory weakness. Central effects include anxiety, confusion, hallucinations, and seizures, and hypothalamic involvement can cause SIADH with hyponatremia. Urine may darken to red-brown on standing as PBG converts to porphobilin and porphyrins. The key laboratory finding during an attack is markedly elevated urine PBG.

blocks.predict: Why does acute intermittent porphyria cause no skin photosensitivity, unlike porphyria cutanea tarda?
blocks.explain: Photosensitivity requires porphyrins, which absorb light and generate reactive oxygen species in skin. The AIP block lies before any porphyrin ring is formed, so ALA and PBG accumulate instead, and these are neurotoxic but not photoactive.
blocks.check: The description of the heme pathway and where the deaminase acts.

blocks.text: Microcephaly is a head circumference more than 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and sex; more than 3 standard deviations is severe. Because the skull grows in response to the growing brain, a small head almost always means a small brain. Brain size depends on how many neurons neural progenitor cells produce during the first and second trimesters and on how well those neurons survive. Anything that kills progenitors, halts their division, or destroys developing neurons in that window can cause microcephaly, so the causes are genetic (single-gene primary microcephaly, chromosomal syndromes), infectious, toxic, and metabolic. Microcephaly present at birth points to injury in utero; acquired microcephaly, in which head growth slows after birth, suggests later injury.

Congenital infections are the best-tested causes. Zika virus has strong tropism for neural progenitor cells and kills them, producing severe microcephaly, sometimes with a collapsed skull and excess scalp skin, along with subcortical calcifications, ventriculomegaly, eye abnormalities, and joint contractures from loss of motor neurons. Cytomegalovirus is the most common congenital infection; it replicates in the germinal matrix around the ventricles, producing periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, and sensorineural hearing loss. Congenital rubella, most damaging in the first trimester, inhibits cell division and damages vessels, causing cataracts, sensorineural deafness, patent ductus arteriosus, and microcephaly. Congenital toxoplasmosis causes diffuse intracranial calcifications and chorioretinitis; it more often causes hydrocephalus, but destructive disease can leave microcephaly.

Ethanol is the most common preventable teratogenic cause. It triggers apoptosis of neural progenitors and disrupts neuronal migration and neural crest cells, producing fetal alcohol syndrome: microcephaly, growth restriction, intellectual disability, and a smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and short palpebral fissures. Maternal PKU, described earlier, injures the fetus through high maternal phenylalanine.

integration.text: The diseases in this chapter share one logic. A single defect, an extra chromosome, a silenced gene, a missing enzyme, or a failed transporter, either removes a needed product (tyrosine, FMRP, ceruloplasmin, heme) or lets a toxic substrate accumulate (phenylalanine, leucine, ammonia, copper, ALA, stored lipid). Anatomy tells you where it lands: substrate collects in the cells that turn it over, so gangliosides fill neurons, sphingomyelin and glucocerebroside fill macrophages, galactolipids destroy myelinating cells, and copper damages the liver before the lenticular nucleus. Genetics explains who is affected: X-linked disorders (adrenoleukodystrophy, Fabry, Hunter, OTC, fragile X) strike boys, with variable disease in heterozygous girls through X inactivation, and the autosomal dominant AIP depends on environmental triggers to become symptomatic.

Timing explains the clinical picture. Metabolic toxins cleared by the placenta (phenylalanine, leucine, ammonia) spare the fetus and injure the newborn once feeding begins, whereas teratogens and congenital infections act in utero and leave microcephaly at birth. Classic exam distinctions rest on single discriminators: hepatosplenomegaly for Niemann-Pick versus Tay-Sachs, corneal clouding for Hurler versus Hunter, orotic acid for OTC versus CPS I deficiency, and adrenal failure for adrenoleukodystrophy. Real patients show wide variation in onset and severity within each disease, so these patterns describe the classic forms rather than every case.

summary: Trisomy 21 usually reflects maternal meiosis I nondisjunction; the extra APP gene causes Alzheimer pathology by about age 40, and endocardial cushion, duodenal, and ligament defects explain AV septal defect, duodenal atresia, and atlantoaxial instability.

Adrenoleukodystrophy is X-linked ABCD1 failure of peroxisomal VLCFA import with demyelination and adrenal insufficiency; metachromatic leukodystrophy (arylsulfatase A, sulfatides) and Krabbe disease (galactocerebrosidase, psychosine, globoid cells) are lysosomal and also demyelinate peripheral nerve.

PKU blocks phenylalanine to tyrosine conversion; high phenylalanine starves the brain of other large neutral amino acids, tyrosine becomes essential, and BH4 defects also impair dopamine and serotonin synthesis.
Maternal hyperphenylalaninemia is teratogenic, causing microcephaly and heart defects in an infant who does not have PKU.
Tay-Sachs (hexosaminidase A, GM2) and Niemann-Pick A (sphingomyelinase) both give a cherry-red macula; only Niemann-Pick has hepatosplenomegaly and foam cells.

Fabry disease is X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency with painful small fiber neuropathy, angiokeratomas, and early stroke; Gaucher types 2 and 3 are neuronopathic; Hurler has corneal clouding and Hunter, X-linked, does not.
Wilson disease is autosomal recessive ATP7B loss: no biliary copper excretion, low ceruloplasmin, high urine copper, lenticular nucleus injury, and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Fragile X is FMR1 CGG expansion above about 200 repeats, with promoter hypermethylation and loss of FMRP; expansion occurs through maternal transmission.
Maple syrup urine disease (branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase) and OTC deficiency (X-linked, hyperammonemia with orotic aciduria) cause neonatal encephalopathy after feeding begins.
AIP is autosomal dominant PBG deaminase deficiency unmasked by ALAS1 inducers, causing neurovisceral attacks with high urine PBG and no photosensitivity.

The statement that Kayser-Fleischer rings occur in nearly all neurologic Wilson cases and about half of hepatic cases reflects common review figures; percentages vary between series.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the age range for childhood cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy (about 4 to 10 years) and the Krabbe onset range (about 3 to 6 months) as stated.
